verdict: Second read confirms the first reader's literal checks: no em-dash, no forbidden word, every exclamation point inside quoted Scripture (Nehemiah 2:3, Psalm 137:5, Psalm 137:9), biography limited to the five sons, right and left criticized with the same instrument and the asymmetry stated. Of six findings, one survives. The other five either sit at a true hinge, do real work in the argument, or offered a replacement that was not clearly better than the original. Nothing was missed on the second pass that I would stake the essay on.

keep.quote: Love comes first, and the improvement follows. That is how Nehemiah loved a city in ruins.
keep.tell: Paragraph restates a quotation as a slogan (aphoristic two-beat gloss)
keep.why: Chesterton's own sentence, quoted immediately before ("She was great because they had loved her"), has just said exactly this. The gloss repeats it in a tidy balanced form, and the paragraph already has its landing in the Nehemiah line.
keep.replacement: That is how Nehemiah loved a city in ruins.

dropped: "Scripture keeps that verse, and it isn't there as a model. It is there because it is true to the human heart." Dropped: this is the hardest verse in the essay and a true hinge, the one place the plain 'not this, that' earns its keep. The proposed replacement changed almost nothing.

"The worshiper believes it nearly is. The despiser never quite forgives the country for being only a country, a mixed and mortal thing." Dropped: the appositive is slightly literary, but it says what 'only a country' means (good and evil together, and not eternal), which the Revelation 21 argument depends on. Cutting it flattens a sentence doing work. Unsure, so left alone.

"Contempt feels like moral seriousness. More often than its owners suspect, it is pride, and underneath the pride is ingratitude." Dropped: a 'consider' finding. The line is a diagnosis with content, and it leads into the next paragraph instead of closing the section.

"What he did next sets the pattern for a Christian love of country: ..." Dropped: a 'consider' finding. It is the plain signposting the brief lists among his habits, the colon introduces a Scripture quotation, and 'He writes,' would remove the claim the section is built on.

"The Christian question is whether Scripture sorts it the same way, and I don't think it does." Dropped: it sounds like a man talking, and the next paragraph commits ("The short answer is yes"). Removing it makes the sentence less human.
for_james: The five-sons paragraph is the most human moment in the piece and stays general (songs, stories, gratitude). One real detail only you have would lift it. None has been invented.
"Perhaps you served, or your father did" addresses the reader and claims nothing about you. Confirm you are comfortable with it.
"She died that August." closes the Weil paragraph as a bare fact. It is accurate (ledger: August 1943). It reads a little like a dramatic kicker; your call whether it stays.
